“Young and beardless, around thirty” describes their youthful appearance, while their understanding, strength, and bodily development are complete.
Mount Uhud is near Medina; al-Bayda is a mountain near Damascus. The report compares the distance to three days' travel.

This recalls the words of revelation: “The life to come is truly the life.” The reason is that the life to come is itself alive and aware. Life and awareness are not extra qualities added to it, as they seem to be in this worldly condition, which resembles sleep. Sleep, after all, is called the brother of death.

Think of what you see in a dream: a sky above you, an earth beneath you, beautiful images that delight you, or disturbing images that frighten and hurt you. All of them exist as forms in your awareness, yet their presence can be powerful. In a confused dream, imagination works upon forms gathered from waking experience. In a true dream, the inner faculty that brings sensations together may witness forms from higher sources and reflect them to the soul, or the soul may know them directly without such a reflection. In every case, what is experienced belongs to knowledge and life.

Pleasure and pain are nothing other than awareness of what suits us or goes against us. What we know immediately is the form present in awareness. So an event outside us is not pleasant or painful simply as an event; it is experienced as pleasant or painful through how it is known.

Even a distressing image need not cause distress by itself. Much of its power comes from what imagination and judgment make of it. The image of losing family or property makes you grieve because imagination treats the loss of your connection to them as though you had lost your very self, or some quality that truly belongs to you.

Similarly, we may fear the image of a dead person who, even when alive, had no power to harm us. Our horror of the corpse comes from imagination. The same is true of our dislike of many things we have learned to find repulsive. It is as though we carve out, for ourselves, the very things that frighten, hurt, sadden, and attack us. What trouble we bring upon ourselves!
Blessed is the person who sees the Lord appearing in both gentleness and severity, and loves Him through all the forms of His names. Such a person finds the greater contentment that comes from God.
The word means numbness or a dulling of sensation, a term also used by physicians.

This is a difficult objection for anyone who claims that a separate soul can suffer bodily-style pain but denies that its inner powers can exist in an imaginal form. A particular image requires a particular power that can perceive and imagine it.

The objection is that there is no special relation to explain why this soul, rather than another, should become attached to this heavenly body, rather than another. Without such a reason, the choice would be arbitrary. It is not being claimed that an earthly soul can have no relation at all to a heavenly body. Someone could answer that even before death the soul is joined to something resembling a heavenly sphere. We have said that the human being contains something corresponding to everything in the world. The very fine vapour within the body, which is the soul's first bodily connection, resembles a heavenly sphere because it is balanced and stands between opposing qualities.

This likeness is why it can be called a ‘sphere.’ Scripture itself speaks of the heavens as ‘smoke.’ On this comparison, the heavens are like the subtle vapour in the head of the greater human being—the world as a whole—while the vapour in a person's own head is the sphere of the small world that a human being contains.
Some philosophers proposed a smoky body as the subject of imagination because the soul's earthly powers depend on subtle bodily fluids, nerves, veins, and related structures.

The proposed body would be composite and so subject to decay, though the realm of the afterlife is everlasting. If it were a simple, indestructible body, it would in effect be another celestial sphere, yet would still be finite and too small to hold an unlimited number of souls.
The objection is about souls gathering all at once, not entering bodies one after another over time.

In the soul's higher state, its power to act returns to its knowledge, somewhat as God's knowledge is active rather than received from things outside Him. Its imagination returns to a power of direct seeing, as happens in dreams—which are said to resemble death. What someone sees, hears, and experiences there can be vivid perception, not merely a faint picture. Here is a fuller account. In this bodily life the soul has ten outward and inward powers. In the world of images there are corresponding powers, since this world receives its reality from that one. But the world of images is wider and is not limited by physical matter, position, or time.

Each power can therefore contain all ten: sight can do the work of all ten, and so can hearing, and so on. This gives a hundred forms of power. At the level of intellect, where the soul is unified more completely, each of these can again be understood in relation to all ten, making a thousand. These are not a thousand separate organs. One soul, precisely because it is one, contains their powers. For this reason it brings forth its many bodily powers as expressions of what is already in it. That is the point of the claim that the visible powers are all shadows of what lies in the soul's own reality.
Scripture asks, ‘Have you not seen how your Lord extends the shadow?’
The manuscript note says the passage seems to promise a second argument against the objection, but no such second argument appears.

Taken literally, this passage and the later words ‘even if they are assumed to be without end’ might suggest that the souls of the deeply unhappy are finite in number. That need not be so. The souls of those nearest to God and the souls of those who have reached the depths of misery may both be without number, not only the many people in between. The world has a beginning, as the stronger argument shows, yet God's giving never comes to an end. His giving is everlasting even though each thing that receives it comes into being. His creative act does not cease, though each created thing begins. God's words do not run out.

Perhaps Sadra is here allowing, for the sake of argument, the view that the suffering of unbelievers will eventually end because they will acquire a nature suited to the Fire, as a salamander is said to be suited to fire. Their souls would then cease to count as unhappy in that sense. He may also be drawing on the view, soon to be quoted from Suhrawardi, that ignorant and immoral people may be delivered through the Greater Spirit.

I see no difficulty in saying that the clear and subtle body of a heavenly sphere can display images belonging to the souls of some of those who have attained happiness. Because it is so clear, forms from the world below can also appear in it. Suhrawardī makes this point in The Philosophy of Illumination: everything in the world of elements, he says, is pictured in the heavens just as it appears here, with all its features. Every human being is shown there with all their states, movements, and moments of rest, whether already past or still to come.

Al-Shīrāzī, explaining another passage by Suhrawardī, says that these pictures of earthly things in the heavenly spheres must recur. If something knows every future event in its proper order, as the souls of the heavenly spheres are said to do, or if all those events are pictured within it, as they are said to be pictured in the heavenly bodies, then the recurrence of those events follows. He accepts the first claim on the basis of the earlier argument, and so accepts the conclusion.

There is no conflict between the claim that these images exist in their own right and the claim that they appear through other things. On the author's account, imagination is independent of matter, while the subtle spirit associated with the brain provides a way for it to appear. The reality imagined and the act of imagining are one at the appropriate level. Similarly, for Suhrawardī, images seen in mirrors and in imagination belong to the independent world of images. Neither the spirit associated with the brain nor a mirror is their material container. Each is only a place where they become visible.

An image that exists independently does not need a mirror in order to be what it is. Its appearing there follows from the mirror's own nature. In the same way, when the soul, at a level beyond ordinary bodily existence, appears with its imagined forms through a heavenly body, that does not make it the soul of that heavenly body. Images appear in polished mirrors because of the mirrors' properties and because of a relation between the soul and the forms seen. This does not make the mirrors living beings with souls. Nor does it prevent heavenly bodies from remaining under the powers proper to their own natures. Thus no movement of one soul into another natural body is required.

Just as the heavens can display the greater world of images, they can display the lesser world of images belonging to individual souls. We should not reject the possibility that a being in the visible world reveals one from the unseen world. After all, the soul belongs to a higher order while its body is a visible, physical thing that reveals it. Imagined forms belong to that higher order too, while the subtle bodily spirit can reveal them. The discussion of resurrection will also establish ways in which Paradise and Hell appear in this world.

The author objects that souls in the next life have no bodies through which they could stand in a spatial relation to the heavens, as an object stands before a mirror. But why could their relation not be like the relation of powers and images to the subtle spirits associated with the brain?

This is how I understand Suhrawardī's statement in The Philosophy of Illumination: some happy souls who have not reached the highest rank, together with people of self-restraint who have freed themselves from bodily attachments, can enter the world of independent images, which appear through certain higher heavenly bodies. They can themselves bring such images into appearance. Food, beautiful sights, pleasing sounds, and whatever they wish become present to them. These forms are more complete than the corresponding forms in our world, because their higher supports are complete while the bodies that support appearances here are limited. These souls remain there because they retain a connection with the higher intervening bodies, which do not decay.

In Suhrawardī's terminology, an intervening body is a natural body. Elsewhere he says that some souls at an intermediate rank may give rise to luminous, independently existing images, displayed through the heavenly spheres, which appear as countless groups of angels. This is also the meaning of an earlier view, attributed by his commentator to Plato and others, about the passage of people who have reached perfection in action. — S. R.

In sleep, the soul produces beautiful images, enjoys them, and is affected by them. It also produces frightening images and suffers fear and pain because of them. These images do not appear for no reason.

In ordinary bodily life, good or poor care, together with the conditions of the body, prepares someone for a particular state of health or illness. One outcome does not occur without something that makes it possible. Nothing comes to be until its causes are in place. Likewise, in waking life, our chosen actions, the body's natural condition, and the bodily spirit prepare the soul to form certain images rather than others. This does not happen through an arbitrary choice without a cause.

So too in the next life: past actions and settled habits bring the soul, through the order of causes, to produce forms suited to what it has become. It cannot simply choose incompatible forms, however strong its powers become, because effects must be suited to their causes. That is why we are told that our deeds will return to us. As Rumi says, in effect: “If a thorn has wounded you, you planted it yourself; if you wear silk, you spun it yourself.”

All higher and lower causes are also means by which God's generosity reaches things and through which He acts. “Say: All is from God.” The real existence of created things does not conflict with God's being the true source of existence. In the same way, their real actions do not conflict with His all-embracing power to act. We must hold both truths together, avoiding either extreme.

We should not picture descent as a straight line and the return as a separate curve. The circle is taken as the best image because it is simple and whole; its center stands in the same relation to every point on its edge. Each level on the descending side has a counterpart on the ascending side. The realities correspond, though their modes of existence differ. On the way down, there are intellects that are immaterial from the beginning. On the way up, there are souls that become fully intellectual only after being freed from matter and its attachments. Souls begin their existence in connection with bodies, even though they continue in a spiritual state.

This helps explain the saying that the bearers of the Throne are four at the beginning but eight at the end: the first four are joined by four others brought forth along the path of the complete human being. The verse says, ‘Eight will bear the Throne of your Lord that Day.’ There are distinctions within each half of the circle, yet all share one reality, because existence is one reality with differing degrees. On the descending side, souls come before the world of images in the timeless order; on the ascending side, souls reach that world after living in time. There is a world of images on each side, and below them are the changing natures that exist in time.

The first intermediate realm is where the covenant with God is taken; the final one is where people meet the results of keeping or breaking that covenant. Philosophers agree that such forms exist, though they disagree about whether they exist independently or in celestial souls.

One might object: a rule of reason cannot cease to apply, so what is impossible must always remain impossible. The reply is that the statement is intended to uphold both reason and revelation. The forms that appear in the afterlife must answer to the forms known in this world, but they do not thereby return to the earthly world. ‘Return in the afterlife’ can mean that worldly forms find their answer there. Or it can mean a return to a world that is directly seen and disclosed, not a return to physical nature as we know it. In the afterlife, forms become fuller, clearer, and more readily known than in the intermediate state after death.

In my copy of the Journey on the Soul, a disputed word appears only in the margin; it may have been added by a later hand. If it is not original, the sentence can be read in another way: precisely because the afterlife is not this world, a return from one to the other is impossible. They are different states, as the goal differs from the way that leads to it.
The comparison between mirror images, dreams, and afterlife images works only if the images are not materially inside the mirror and if the soul is connected to the image so that it is alive.

Avicenna points out that people marvel when a magnet pulls iron, yet take for granted the soul's power to move the body—making it rise, descend, walk, run, or fall. The note also quotes Persian verse about how imagination shapes conflict and honor, while our strength comes from an unseen wind.

You may ask: how does this account agree with the belief that the Prophet ascended to heaven in his body? I answer that the discussion here is not about prophetic souls or miracles. In the case of Muhammad, the final Prophet, the ascent did not involve his coarse, heavy body as a coarse body. His body was subtle. A body that can see behind itself as clearly as in front, and that casts no shadow, cannot be dense in the ordinary way. It is subtler even than the outermost heavenly sphere. Yet the body with which he ascended was his outward, actual body.

Later, in the discussion of bodily resurrection, the author will say that the body raised on the last day is this same body that lived in the world. Bodily ascent and bodily resurrection go together; they are, so to speak, twins nourished at the same breast, and many of the same principles govern them.

How could a philosopher who knows divine realities say that the Prophet ascended only in spirit, not in body? In one sense, the ascent of the spirit includes that of the body, because the deeper reality contains its outward expression. The spirit's ascent therefore carries with it the ascent of what expresses it. This is even clearer for the body that appears in the world of images. But someone who truly knows these matters should not stop at saying that the body is included in the spirit. That person should also affirm that the Prophet's outward body itself ascended.

It is useful here to give a brief account of the ascent, though a full account would go beyond the purpose of this note. Many reports describe it, and the Qur'an refers to it in the verse beginning, “Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque.” Gabriel brought the Prophet the creature called Burāq, with a saddle and bridle set with precious jewels and wings like those of birds. When the Prophet first approached to ride, Burāq shied and ran away. Gabriel brought it back, and the Messenger of God mounted it.

A ladder with steps extending from earth to heaven then appeared. Through it the Prophet ascended, stage by stage, seeing the heavens and what they contain. Later the Burāq was replaced by the rafraf, on which he rose still farther. Gabriel reached the limit of his strength, but the Prophet continued to the innermost place of divine majesty, where God revealed to His servant what He revealed and he saw what he saw. The reports supply the remaining details.

Muslims have differed greatly about the nature of this event. Some, citing reports attributed to ʿĀʾisha and Muʿāwiya, say it took place in a dream. I regard that claim as false. Others say it happened while he was awake, but only in spirit. Others accept that he traveled in his body as far as the Farthest Mosque, as the Qur'an explicitly states, but deny that his body rose beyond heaven. I also reject this last view. The ascent to heaven itself has become a firmly established belief of the religion. A belief established in that way does not depend on our recovering a separate proof for every part of it. Its detailed features, however, are drawn from the reports.

Most Muslims maintain that the Prophet was awake and traveled bodily from the Sacred Mosque to a place above the heavens. Some spiritual teachers and philosophers also accept that the event happened while he was awake, but understand the body involved as a body of the world of images. They take everything he saw as an image with a real meaning, following accounts such as those of Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn Arabi on the forms of the afterlife and of Suhrawardī on the world of reflected images. They hold that every meaning can take a form and every higher reality has an outward expression.

On this interpretation, what people traveling toward God see must be understood through its inner meaning, much as a dream must be interpreted. Traveling from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque is a visible form of moving from one spiritual station to another. The prophets' following Muhammad in prayer represents the followers of his community, heirs of the prophets, taking him as their guide. Burāq represents the acts of worship that carry a person forward, as in the saying, “Prayer is the believer's ascent.”

The saddle and bridle represent a gathered, attentive mind and a heart present in worship. The jewels represent love, sincerity, humility, and reverence. Burāq's shying away represents a passing, bodily or human thought. Gabriel's bringing it back represents the removal of that thought by the universal intellect, which directs the Prophet toward what is right—or by the Prophet's own spiritual reality. The rafraf represents the joining of unity and multiplicity, and of spiritual and natural qualities, through taking on qualities that reflect the One of whom it is said, “Nothing is like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.”

Gabriel's visible form, resembling Diḥya al-Kalbī, represents the universal intellect and is an expression of the Holy Spirit. Gabriel's growing weary and being unable to go farther represents the Prophet's superiority even to the angels nearest to God. He passes beyond them to a station that no other being can enter, the station described as “or nearer still.” The Prophet expressed this by saying, “I have a time with God in which neither an angel brought near nor a prophet sent forth can accompany me.” ʿAṭṭār of Nishapur puts it well:
When He makes a celebration in solitude with His friend, Gabriel's wings burn; he cannot enter.
When the great bird of his soul appears, Even Moses is left startled and small.

The other details may be interpreted in the same way. But do not mistake this view for the claim that the ascent happened only in spirit. Those who say it was purely spiritual do not suppose that the Prophet saw these actual images at all. For them, the ascent is simply the progress of the prophetic spirit through higher levels of understanding. Climbing the heavens means advancing by thought and knowledge; Burāq is a metaphor for obedience; and the saddle, bridle, and jewels stand for keeping the heart free of selfish thoughts and open to angelic and divine inspiration. They are not forms the traveler actually sees.

A person engaged in prayerful attention and spiritual struggle may, however, really see images of that struggle: perhaps a battlefield on which armies of light pursue armies of darkness. Another person may undergo the same struggle without seeing any such image. This experience does not come to everyone. It depends on the strength of a person's spiritual practice and insight, and on the rank of prophecy or sainthood reached.

The truth, in my view, is that the Prophet ascended while awake, with his noble outward body, to a place above the heavens, and with his holy spirit to the innermost divine presence, to the station “or nearer still.” Those who deny a bodily ascent raise several objections. The strongest relies on the philosophers' claim that the heavenly spheres cannot be split open and then joined together again.

Many theologians, including the careful thinker al-Lāhījī in Gawhar-i Murād, therefore said that this impossibility applies only to the outermost sphere. The reports speak of the Prophet ascending above the heavens, and the religious accounts count seven heavens, with the Throne and Footstool beyond them. They argued that the reason breaking and rejoining cannot occur is that the outermost sphere sets the bounds of direction. To break it would require direction to be fixed independently of what fixes direction. On this reasoning, the impossibility would apply only to that outermost sphere.

I am surprised that so skilled a thinker should have said this. A heavenly sphere, in the philosophy under discussion, is a simple body with a fifth kind of nature, whose natural tendency is circular rather than straight movement. If it could receive the tendency toward straight movement, or the associated features of heat, cold, expansion, and contraction, it would no longer be a heavenly sphere. What would then distinguish it from an earthly element? The distinction rests precisely on these two kinds of natural motion. Showing that one proof of impossibility applies only to the sphere that sets the bounds of direction does not remove every other proof. Denying a particular reason is not the same as denying every reason.

The better answer is that the Prophet's bodily ascent through even the outermost sphere required no breaking at all. His body was so subtle that it could pass through the heavenly bodies without splitting them. I have described only a small part of its subtlety at the beginning of this note.

Even people who practise the arts of preparing substances know of oils that, when placed on the palm, are said to penetrate to the back of the hand because of their fineness. They also speak of highly refined substances called spirits, produced through repeated distillation and rising vapours, which penetrate denser substances called bodies as though they pass through them at once.

Consider a vessel filled with earth. No more earth may fit, yet it can still hold a substantial amount of water. Fill it with water, and there may still be room for air. A skin filled with air may still receive fire, in the account of the elements used here. The same reasoning can be extended, hypothetically, from fire to a heavenly sphere, and from a lower sphere to a higher one. The finer substance can pass through the denser one. The body of the final Prophet, the center around which the spheres turn, is subtler than they are. It is therefore no wonder that it could pass through them without tearing them apart.

Some say that he ascended in the body of the world of images, but not in his outward body. They would not say this if they fully understood the relation between the two. It is like the relation between an image supported by a surface and a reality that stands by itself. What stands by itself possesses in full the perfections expressed in what depends on something else; it does not lose any of its positive reality.

Another objection is drawn from the Qur'anic passage in which unbelievers demand that the Prophet make a spring gush from the ground, produce a garden of palms and vines with rivers running through it, cause pieces of the sky to fall, bring God and the angels before them, possess a house of gold, or rise into heaven—and even then they say they will not believe in his ascent until he brings down a book they can read. He is told to reply, “Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?” Some take this to deny that a human being can ascend bodily.

But the expression of wonder concerns their demand that he bring God before them, not the possibility of rising into heaven. Bodily ascent is no more opposed to his humanity than having a garden of palms and grapes would be. The same answer applies to their other weak objections. What I shall explain about bodily resurrection will also help us understand bodily ascent. — S. R.
As the soul turns toward its higher life, it pays less attention to keeping the body in good condition, and the body gradually deteriorates.

You may object that many people fear death and care for their bodies more intensely as it approaches. A sacred report even says that God does not hesitate over anything as He does over taking the soul of a believing servant: the servant dislikes death, and God dislikes causing the servant distress.

The answer is that the turn toward the higher life, and the wish to rely less on the body and its powers, belong to the soul's rational nature and deepest aim. They do not rule out the imagination's fear of bodily death. Imagination and bodily apprehension are, in one respect, other than the soul's rational nature. In short, the wish to leave behind dependence on the body is a wish for completeness and self-sufficiency. Reason naturally seeks this, even when imagination shrinks from dying.
“All beings” here means the beings of the natural world, which move toward God in different ways. It does not mean that every soul is a separate intelligence.

Among the great mystics, a divine name means the reality of existence considered through one of God's attributes. Consider existence as something that appears in itself and makes other things appear: it is called Light. Consider it as what reveals both itself and everything else: it is called the Knowing One. Consider it as beautiful and good, rejoicing in itself and in its own effects, loving and approving them because they come from it: it is called the Willing, the Loving, and the Content. Consider it as giving existence knowingly and by choice: it is called the Powerful. Other divine names can be explained in the same way. ‘Name’ may also refer to any created thing insofar as it is a sign of some perfection of God.

With this in mind, the statement that the two groups travel and come to rest ‘in God's name’ means that the wind, the person steering, those who follow, the soul, and the soul's powers all act as signs of God's power. The journey begins through His name as the source that brings things forth, and comes to rest through His name as the final end to which they return. The mystics regard the divine names as the real sources of the kinds of things in the world. Where others see the works of bodily powers, natural forces, souls, and intellects, they see the effects of God's beautiful names.
The commentator suggests that the author may have left out another version of the “one soul” view for brevity, or because it was too weak to mention.
The argument assumes that each feature must exist separately. The commentator replies that a thing can contain several features in one unified existence.

Powers can separate even when they are in the same bodily place, as when one bodily function fails while another remains. But the argument is about distinct souls, not merely distinct powers. Their differences can also come from the different stages and roles of a living thing.
The commentator clarifies the grammar of this sentence: it introduces the condition that there must be a shared source for the powers.
The objection would work only if “cause” meant “manifestation” in the special sense used by some mystics. That is not the sense used in this argument.

The soul is what performs all these actions. Yet the soul is not material, while the actions in question have some connection with matter. It therefore needs different bodily organs, each of which directs the soul's activity towards a particular task.

Without these organs, its activity would not be directed in this specific way. And without that direction, no particular action would take place: considered simply in itself, an immaterial agent has an equal relation to all material things. This is, in substance, what the author will say near the end of the discussion. Seen this way, the objection raises a genuine point, but its supporters have not explained it with enough care.
Individual sense images prepare the soul to know particular things. The soul itself is not a storehouse of separate bodily images.

The commentator distinguishes physical multiplicity, such as division into places and shapes, from differences in meaning. Intellectual beings can contain many meanings without being divided into parts.

Take anger as an example. It is one reality appearing at different levels. In the bodily world, it may appear as the blood growing hot, the face darkening, and the veins swelling. In the soul, it is an inward state free from those bodily features, moving a person to seek relief or revenge. At the level of intellect, it corresponds to the power to overcome, as shown by the higher lights separate from matter. At the divine level, it points to the absolute power that prevails over all lesser lights, the overwhelming majesty of the Light of Lights before which all multiplicity fades.

Love, mercy, fear, and similar states can be understood in the same way. This example concerns states of feeling. Knowledge also appears differently at different levels: whiteness is present to sight in one way, to imagination in another, and to intellect in another. The same is true of beings themselves. The human being has a natural, bodily existence, an existence in the world of images, an intellectual existence, and a higher existence; and within the mind it can be understood as this particular sensory image, an image in imagination, a general intellectual concept, or a universal nature applying to all these levels.
The commentator extends the comparison: the ten outer and inner senses are present in the imaginal world in many combinations, and in the intellectual world in an even more unified way.
Many meanings can be true of one simple being without breaking its unity.

In short, what is true of the receiver affects what it receives, and what is true of what is received affects the receiver. The soul brings its own awareness to its powers and their bodily instruments. The body, however, imposes limits and particular conditions on how that awareness appears. Because an organ is limited, it cannot display every quality of the soul.

An objection may be raised. If the bodily world is divided into parts, should not every power of the single soul appear in every organ, even if only faintly? Why should one organ see and another hear?

The answer is that division alone does not explain the differences. The organs also have different bodily makeups, materials, positions, and relationships. That is why the soul appears as sight in the eye and as hearing in the ear, even though every part of reality may in one respect contain something of every other part.

There is a deeper answer. The soul is a great sign of reality, and it shows qualities of both transcendence and likeness. It has levels: meanings free from particular limits, meanings understood in relation to something else, forms free from matter, and forms joined to matter. Some of its powers are one without occupying places; others are divided through position and bodily organs. These differences belong to their respective levels. The human soul therefore has a genuine, reflected unity, not the numerical unity of a thing counted as one part among others.
The soul's need for different powers and organs shows that it is at a lower stage than the separate intellect. When the soul no longer needs them, it has become intellect.
The claim that the soul cannot be one because it acts both with and without matter is not decisive if existence can grow stronger by stages and the soul can change in its very being.
“Fully present knowledge” here means knowledge at the level of the acquired intellect.
The argument includes imagination among the powers said to perceive bodily things.
This refers to the earlier argument that different powers can be separated.
One source can produce one effect when the body's readiness is present, and no effect when it is absent. These are different conditions, not different sources.
If the Giver of Forms alone caused every effect and the powers only prepared the body, then active powers would not be needed. The commentator says this would make them useless.

The disagreement here concerns demonstration, not merely a contest of opinions. The illuminationist philosopher argues according to his own principles, while the author argues both from his principles and from those of the philosophers in Aristotle’s school. One example is the author's acceptance of substantial forms joined to matter and responsible for things' distinctive effects. The philosopher of illumination, by contrast, speaks of forms separate from matter that act upon it: the governing beings he calls the lords of species.

The author is right that the unity of God, both in Himself and in His action, does not require us to deny created powers. Powers joined to physical things are instruments through which God acts. The higher beings that are separate from matter are also His instruments, or, in another image, eyes through which His governance is displayed. Scripture itself speaks of God's hosts and describes Him as exalted in rank and Lord of the Throne.
On the illuminationist account, the single reality does not differ in level, still less in number or kind. Its differences arise from the ways it appears to receivers with different capacities.

An objection arises: the philosopher of illumination also speaks of powers. What can he mean by them if, throughout the body, only the soul acts? Consider the imagination. For the author, it is the soul appearing as a particular active power, able to perceive images free from matter though not from size. The power that forms bodily shapes, or the power by which a plant grows, is likewise the soul operating in a particular way without leaving its higher level. In the illuminationist account, imagination can instead be understood as the soul or intellect appearing through a receptive power joined to a bodily condition. The same can be said of the other powers. In this sense it is reasonable to say that the illuminationist philosopher did not abolish powers altogether.
Even the ancient philosophers discussed here held that imagination can exist apart from the natural body. It is linked to the imaginal world, not simply to a bodily organ.

Differences between kinds of living things come from their active sources; differences between individuals come from the matter that receives a form. Matter makes an individual distinct, but it does not create the kind itself.
Bodily powers are real natural causes. God is the ultimate source of existence, but these powers act directly within nature.
